# Particle and Feature-Based Methods

Also called: Particle-based isosurface extraction, Fiber Surface Extraction

## Overview
Particle and Feature-Based Methods extract [isosurfaces](#13788-isosurfaces.md) from discrete [particle systems](#20144-particle-systems.md) or bivariate vector fields, bypassing the need for a dense scalar grid. This family solves the high computational cost and memory bottlenecks associated with traditional grid-based extraction for dynamic, unbounded, or vector-valued data [S1]. Unlike standard Marching Cubes which operates on a dense grid, these methods extract surfaces directly from particle positions or range-space projections, enabling real-time performance for complex entities like fluid blobs or fiber tracts [S1].

## Shared principles
The family relies on the topological logic of the parent [Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration](2518-marching-cubes-lookup-and-configuration.md), specifically the use of the `edgeTable` and `triangleTable` to determine connectivity and triangulation based on vertex classifications. However, the definition of "vertex value" and the method of determining edge intersections are generalized:
1.  **Implicit Field Evaluation**: Instead of reading from a precomputed grid, field values are computed on-the-fly. For particles, this involves summing radial basis functions (e.g., $f(r)$) from nearby particles [S1]. For vector fields, this involves evaluating the vector function $f(x)$ at grid vertices [S1].
2.  **Range-Space Projection**: In feature-based extraction, the [binary classification](#931-binary-classification.md) of vertices (inside/outside) is determined by mapping domain vertices to the range space and performing point-in-polygon tests against a control polygon [S1].
3.  **Edge Intersection via Range**: Edge intersections are not found by scalar interpolation. Instead, the line segment connecting the range-space projections of the edge endpoints is intersected with the boundary of the target feature (isosurface or control polygon) to determine the interpolation parameter $t$ [S1].

## Subtopics

### [Real-time particle isosurface extraction](10275-real-time-particle-isosurface-extraction.md)
[Real-time particle isosurface extraction](#10275-real-time-particle-isosurface-extraction.md) is a technique for the fast, high-quality polygonization of isosurfaces generated by thousands of particles in an unbounded spatial domain, using minimal working memory. It sets itself apart from standard Marching Cubes by operating on discrete particle positions rather than a dense grid, utilizing [block subdivision](#8959-block-subdivision.md) and slice-by-slice extraction to manage memory. It is chosen when rendering dynamic particle systems (e.g., fluid blobs) where grid construction is prohibitive. See [Real-time particle isosurface extraction](10275-real-time-particle-isosurface-extraction.md).

### [Fiber Surface Extraction](14192-fiber-surface-extraction.md)
[Fiber Surface Extraction](#14192-fiber-surface-extraction.md) generalizes [isosurface extraction](#30-isosurface-extraction.md) from univariate scalar fields to bivariate vector fields by extracting the preimage of a curve in the range space. It sets itself apart from standard Marching Cubes by replacing the scalar isovalue comparison with a point-in-polygon test in the range space and computing edge intersections via range-space line intersection rather than scalar interpolation. It is chosen for visualizing vector fields such as fiber tracts or flow lines. See [Fiber Surface Extraction](14192-fiber-surface-extraction.md).

### Feature Location (Particle Initialization)
Feature Location is the initialization step for particle-based rendering, placing particles near a user-selected isosurface. It is defined by sampling volume data at a user-defined grid and creating particles between grid points $r$ and neighbors $n$ if the iso-surface is crossed [S1]. On the GPU, each shader thread compares a grid point's value to its front, right, and top neighbors, outputting 0–3 particle positions into a texture buffer object [S1]. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of grid points [S1].

## Background
The concept of [particle-based volume rendering](#4247-particle-based-volume-rendering-pbvr.md) and feature location was introduced by van Pelt, Vilanova, and van de Wetering in 2008 [S1]. Their work, "GPU-based Particle Systems for Illustrative Volume Rendering," proposed using GPGPU to initialize particles near features and subsequently redistribute them to the isosurface using energy minimization. This approach aimed to enable real-time exploration of volume data by leveraging the parallelism of graphics hardware for both initialization and rendering [S1].
